display-multiple-time-zone-columns-googl.title: Show additional time zones in Google Calendar and Outlook
display-multiple-time-zone-columns-googl.short: Display 2 or 3 Time Zones on Grid
display-multiple-time-zone-columns-googl.description: Add parallel time-zone rulers in Google Calendar and Outlook. Check classic Outlook version limits, labels and the view without changing event times.
display-multiple-time-zone-columns-googl.lede: Extra time-zone rulers let you read one meeting slot in several cities without editing the meeting. Google documents a primary, secondary and tertiary zone. Outlook controls differ by version; do not apply the classic Outlook limit to every Outlook client.

sections.heading: Google Calendar: additional rulers or the world clock
body: On a computer, open Settings, then General and Time zone. Google documents Show additional time zones, a Secondary time zone and an optional Tertiary time zone. Return to an hourly calendar view and inspect the parallel labels.
For other cities, General > World clock offers Show world clock and Add time zone. This is a sidebar clock, a different display from an extra calendar ruler.

sections.heading: Outlook: identify the client before following its menus
body: In new Outlook and Outlook on the web, Microsoft documents Settings > Calendar > View, then Add time zone. Choose the city under Other time zones, optionally give it a label, enable Show in calendar and save. Move up and Move down reorder the additional zones. The cited page does not establish a maximum of three for these clients; its web instructions explicitly discuss three or more.

For classic Outlook, use File > Options > Calendar > Time zones. Microsoft says the latest Outlook for Microsoft 365 supports up to three zones; other classic versions, including Outlook 2019 LTSC and Outlook 2016, support two. Use the second/third-zone checkboxes actually available in that version.
Microsoft says the second zone is visible in day or week view. If a label disappears in another view, return to Day or Week before changing event data.

sections.heading: Worked winter check: three offices, one instant
body: For this author-calculated example, use January 15, 2026 and 08:00 in Los Angeles. That is 16:00 UTC, 11:00 in New York and 16:00 in London. All three labels describe one instant.

With illustrative working hours of 08:00–18:00 in each city, the shared interval is 08:00–10:00 Los Angeles, 11:00–13:00 New York and 16:00–18:00 London: two hours. This is a calculation for the stated date and hours, not a measurement of anyone’s availability.

sections.heading: Verify a ruler without moving a meeting
body: Record one harmless event’s date and start, add the display columns, and compare that same event. Adding a secondary display label is different from changing the event’s own time zone.
Changing the primary display zone can move where events appear on your grid; verify the saved event instant rather than assuming a different visible hour means the meeting was rescheduled.

comparison.heading: January 15, 2026: one row read in three cities

practical: Identify the Outlook client and version.
Use named city zones and short, meaningful labels.
Return to an hourly Day or Week view to inspect additional rulers.
Compare a known event before editing any meeting.

faq.q: Does new Outlook have the same three-zone limit as classic Outlook?
faq.a: The cited Microsoft page gives a three-zone limit for the latest classic Outlook for Microsoft 365, not a universal cap for new Outlook or web. Use the controls in your current client.

faq.q: Does adding a second ruler change a saved meeting?
faq.a: It adds another way to read the same instant. Changing an event’s own time zone is a separate edit.

non-integer-30-and-45-minute-utc-offset-.title: Half-hour and quarter-hour time zones: calculate a meeting that fits
non-integer-30-and-45-minute-utc-offset-.description: Check dated meeting conversions for India, Nepal, Newfoundland and Adelaide. Calculate overlap from local working hours instead of assuming whole-hour offsets.
non-integer-30-and-45-minute-utc-offset-.lede: An hour line in London need not be an hour line in India or Nepal. Use the date and named city zone, then check the whole meeting against each person’s working hours. Fractional offsets and seasonal changes both matter.

sections.heading: Use a city and date, not an offset remembered from another season
body: IANA maintains civil time-zone rules. The calculations here use Python zoneinfo with the installed 2026e-rearguard database and named zones. They are worked examples, not live availability checks; future rule changes can change results.

RFC 5545 section 3.3.14 permits minute components in UTC offsets. That does not mean a DATE-TIME can be written with an arbitrary numeric offset: section 3.3.5 distinguishes UTC, floating time and a local time with TZID. Use those valid forms when inspecting an ICS file.

sections.heading: A meeting can start inside working hours and end outside them
body: On January 15, 2026, 12:00–13:00 London is 17:30–18:30 Kolkata. If the Kolkata workday ends at 18:00, half the meeting lies outside it. Moving the London slot to 11:30–12:30 produces 17:00–18:00 in Kolkata.

Google’s working-hours help documents the feature for work or school accounts and notes that an administrator may not enable it. Configuring those hours helps collaborators schedule; the arithmetic alone does not guarantee that every client displays a warning or rejects an invitation.

sections.heading: Find the intersection, not just the converted start
body: For each city, convert both ends of an assumed 09:00–18:00 workday to the same reference zone. The overlap starts at the later start and ends at the earlier end. If the end is no later than the start, there is no positive overlap.
The table applies that calculation to London and each city separately on January 15 and July 15, 2026. These are pairwise windows; they are not one window shared by all five cities.

sections.heading: Check the minute boundary before sending
body: India and Nepal differ by 15 minutes: 10:00 Kolkata is 10:15 Kathmandu on these dates. A whole-hour London start maps to :30 in Kolkata and :45 in Kathmandu. To reach an exact hour in Kathmandu, use :15 in London on these dates.
Inspect the saved start and end with the recipient’s city zone. Do not assume your calendar offers a specific 15-minute grid control; enter exact times in its supported editor if needed.

comparison.heading: Pairwise 09:00–18:00 working hours, calculated for two dates

practical: Use an exact date and named city zone.
Convert the full start–end interval.
Intersect the two local workdays.
Confirm a suitable slot with the recipient; a calculated overlap is not a booking.

faq.q: What is the London–Adelaide overlap for 09:00–18:00 workdays?
faq.a: On January 15, 2026 there is none. On July 15 there is half an hour, 09:00–09:30 London / 17:30–18:00 Adelaide. Different hours or dates require a fresh calculation.

faq.q: Do fractional zones always shift every meeting by 30 minutes?
faq.a: No. Compare both zones on the date. India and Nepal differ by 15 minutes; two half-hour-offset zones can differ by a whole number of hours.

calendar-week-numbers-iso-monday-versus-.title: Calendar week numbers disagree: compare the year rule and first weekday
calendar-week-numbers-iso-monday-versus-.description: Diagnose different week numbers with dated examples. Separate ISO week years, the first weekday and a January 1 rule before changing calendar events.
calendar-week-numbers-iso-monday-versus-.lede: Two calendars can show the same appointment date with different week labels. Compare both the first weekday and the rule for week 1. A Sunday-first grid alone does not tell you which numbering rule the calendar uses.

sections.heading: Separate two settings before comparing numbers
body: ISO weeks start Monday, and week 1 contains January 4. RFC 5545 section 3.3.10 defines BYWEEKNO using a first-week rule of at least four days, with WKST identifying the start of the week. A Sunday WKST is not, by itself, a command to make the week containing January 1 be week 1.

For comparison, this article defines a different illustrative convention: Sunday-start weeks, with the week containing January 1 counted as week 1. These are explicit calculation assumptions, not a claim that every US calendar or Outlook installation uses them.

sections.heading: Use dates that expose both differences
body: January 4, 2026 is a Sunday. It is the last day of ISO 2026-W01, but the first day of week 2 in the illustrative Sunday/January-1 convention. On Monday January 5, both label the date week 2.

January 1, 2027 is a Friday in ISO 2026-W53. Monday January 4 is ISO 2027-W01, but week 2 under the Sunday/January-1 convention. At the year boundary, compare the week-year as well as the number; subtracting 53 from 1 does not describe a useful one-week offset.

sections.heading: Use an explicit lookup instead of an all-year slogan
body: The table lists individual dates. It deliberately avoids claiming that the two numbers differ by exactly one on every day of 2027: Sundays and week-year rollover require their own check.
ISO 2026 has 53 weeks: week 53 runs December 28, 2026–January 3, 2027. ISO 2027 week 1 starts January 4. The calculated boundaries explain the labels without moving any events.

sections.heading: Inspect app controls without assuming they share a week-year policy
body: Apple’s iPhone guide separates Week Numbers from Start Week On. The former displays labels and the latter changes the first displayed weekday. That source does not establish that changing the first column selects every alternative week-numbering algorithm.
Check the help for your installed calendar and version for a first-week-of-year option. The cited sources do not establish a universal Outlook menu path for that setting.
When arranging a meeting, write the date as well as a week label, for example Monday January 4, 2027 (ISO 2027-W01). Do not reschedule an appointment to make two screen badges agree.

comparison.heading: Worked dates under two explicitly defined rules

practical: Compare the same exact calendar date.
Record the first weekday and the week-1 rule separately.
Check the week-year near December and January.
Put an explicit date in shared plans.

faq.q: Does a Sunday-first grid always mean January 1 is in week 1?
faq.a: No. First weekday and first-week rule are different decisions. Identify both.

faq.q: Should I move an event if its week number differs?
faq.a: Compare its actual saved date and time first. A different display convention is not evidence that the appointment moved.

monthly-recurring-last-weekday-byday-min.title: Last weekday of the month or the 31st? Check the recurrence rule
monthly-recurring-last-weekday-byday-min.short: Last Weekday of Month vs Fixed 31st
monthly-recurring-last-weekday-byday-min.description: Compare the 31st, last calendar day, last Friday and final Monday–Friday date. See the 2026 results and why weekday rules do not exclude public holidays.
monthly-recurring-last-weekday-byday-min.lede: The 31st, the last calendar day and the last Monday–Friday date are different recurrence requests. An RFC 5545 rule targeting day 31 skips months without it. A weekday-only rule excludes weekends, but does not know your public holidays.

sections.heading: Invalid dates are skipped, not rolled back
body: RFC 5545 section 3.3.10 says recurrence instances with invalid dates are ignored and not counted. FREQ=MONTHLY;BYMONTHDAY=31 therefore produces seven dates in a full 2026 year: January, March, May, July, August, October and December 31.

Do not confuse that rule with BYMONTHDAY=-1, which selects the final date of every month. If expressing an all-day start in an ICS file, use DTSTART;VALUE=DATE:20260131 rather than an eight-digit value with the default DATE-TIME type.

sections.heading: Four patterns answer four different questions
body: FREQ=MONTHLY;BYMONTHDAY=31 selects the 31st where it exists. FREQ=MONTHLY;BYMONTHDAY=-1 selects the last calendar date. FREQ=MONTHLY;BYDAY=-1FR selects the last Friday.

FREQ=MONTHLY;BYDAY=MO,TU,WE,TH,FR;BYSETPOS=-1 selects the final Monday–Friday date from that month’s weekday set. It does not exclude a public holiday or a personal day off. Do not present it as a universal last business-day rule.

sections.heading: Read the calculated 2026 dates before choosing
body: The table is calculated from Gregorian month lengths and weekdays. Four 2026 month ends fall on weekends: January 31, February 28, May 31 and October 31. The final Monday–Friday date moves back in those months.
In March, the last Friday is March 27, but the final Monday–Friday date is Tuesday March 31. That difference matters when the requirement is truly the final weekday rather than a Friday meeting.

sections.heading: Check the editor and save a disposable example
body: Apple’s Mac guide documents Custom repeat, Frequency and an On the pattern, including the last weekday of a month. Microsoft’s cited guide documents monthly specific-day and ordinal-weekday examples. Google’s guide documents choosing a repeat frequency and end, without listing every raw RRULE its editor or importer preserves.

Use the options actually present in the app, then inspect the next several saved dates. A standard’s ability to express a rule is not proof that every app exposes, imports or preserves it unchanged. Use a disposable calendar before relying on a complex imported rule.

comparison.heading: Verified 2026 Monthly Resolution Table: BYMONTHDAY=31 vs BYMONTHDAY=-1 vs BYDAY=-1FR vs Last Mon–Fri Date (BYSETPOS=-1)

practical: Write whether the requirement means last date, last Friday or last Monday–Friday date.
Check a short month and a weekend month end.
Apply a separately confirmed holiday policy if needed.
Verify saved occurrences in the source account and recipient app.

faq.q: Does the final weekday rule avoid holidays?
faq.a: No. MO,TU,WE,TH,FR excludes Saturdays and Sundays only. A holiday on a weekday still matches unless handled separately.

faq.q: Why is a monthly-on-31 rule missing in April?
faq.a: April has no 31st. RFC 5545 ignores that invalid recurrence date rather than moving it to April 30.

google-calendar-task-deadline-versus-sch.title: Google task deadline or work block? Reserve the time before it is due
google-calendar-task-deadline-versus-sch.short: Task Deadline vs Scheduled Work Block
google-calendar-task-deadline-versus-sch.description: Separate a Google task deadline from start and end times. Plan three work blocks, check Busy availability and verify what the booking tool actually reads.
google-calendar-task-deadline-versus-sch.lede: A deadline tells you when work is due; it does not estimate or reserve the time needed to finish it. Google Calendar separately documents a task’s deadline, planned start and time spent. Use that distinction to plan the work, then verify availability in the calendar or booking tool that matters.

sections.heading: Google’s deadline is a date, not an hourly reservation
body: Google’s task settings guide says Deadline is the date you expect to complete the task and appears in the All day section. Its deadline notification is at 09:00 local time on that date. Record an exact contractual cut-off in the description or a separate timed deadline event if needed; an all-day date marker is not an encoded 17:00 cut-off.

Start date and time lets you specify the start and how much time you plan to spend. Advanced settings offers Free or Busy; Do not disturb and Automatically decline meetings are work/school options. The same guide says recurring tasks cannot have an end time.

sections.heading: Do not confuse a Google task with an ICS promise
body: RFC 5545 describes VTODO, including optional DTSTART and DUE, separately from VEVENT. Its TRANSP property applies to VEVENT. These standard component definitions do not prove how Google exports its current timed tasks or how a third-party booking system treats them.

Google documents Busy timed tasks within its own interface. If another system reads calendar events rather than Tasks, test the specific connection. A Busy event is information for availability; it does not universally prevent a person from inviting you or guarantee that every connected service checks that calendar.

sections.heading: Worked plan: 270 minutes before Friday’s cut-off
body: Assume a report is due Friday November 13, 2026 at 17:00 and needs 270 minutes of work. Schedule three 90-minute sessions: Tuesday November 10, 09:30–11:00; Wednesday November 11, 14:00–15:30; and Thursday November 12, 09:00–10:30. These are illustrative available times, not dates checked against a real person’s meetings or local holidays.

The three blocks total 4.5 hours. Thursday 10:30 to Friday 17:00 is 30.5 hours. Keep the Friday task deadline date, record the 17:00 requirement explicitly, and check the source calendar for conflicts before committing the blocks.

sections.heading: Choose the execution item and verify its effect
body: For a one-off task in Google Calendar, inspect its start/end and Advanced settings availability. For repeated work requiring a duration, consider a recurring event instead of assuming a repeating task supports an end time.

Google Focus time is a separate feature for eligible work/school accounts. The official guide requires Day or Week view and specific start/end times, and documents meeting-decline settings. A normal Busy event is not automatically the same as Focus time with decline enabled.
Check a neutral work block from the actual scheduling or booking flow. Confirm that the relevant calendar is included, the time is treated as unavailable, and details have the intended visibility.

comparison.heading: Three sessions in the illustrative report plan

practical: Estimate effort independently of the due date.
Inspect task start/end and Free/Busy.
Check plan and account eligibility for automatic decline.
Test the actual availability consumer.

faq.q: Why did a deadline notify me at 09:00?
faq.a: Google documents a 09:00 local-time notification on the deadline date. Add an earlier planned work session if you need to start sooner.

faq.q: Does marking an event Busy reject all meeting invitations?
faq.a: No universal rejection follows from Busy. Automatic decline is a separate supported setting; verify the specific account and feature.

backward-planning-project-deadlines-acro.title: Plan backward across weekends and days off: a counted example
backward-planning-project-deadlines-acro.description: Count a project backward from a dated deadline. State whether the final day counts, skip the chosen days off and verify every stage before creating work blocks.
backward-planning-project-deadlines-acro.lede: Before subtracting business days, define which days can be worked and whether the deadline date itself counts. A calendar cannot infer your organisation’s holidays or how a contract counts days. This is an illustrative planning method, not a legal deadline calculator.

sections.heading: Choose the counting convention first
body: For this example, working days are Monday–Friday except November 11, 2026, which this fictional team has explicitly chosen as a day off. Do not assume that date is a holiday for every reader. The deadline is Friday November 20 at 17:00 and includes a full final workday.

If the cut-off were Friday at 09:00, Friday would not supply a full working day before it. Agree that convention before placing the first work block. For formal filing or contractual deadlines, use the governing rule rather than this generic example.

sections.heading: Count dates one by one when exclusions exist
body: Starting at the chosen final eligible day, count it, step backward one date, skip every weekend or listed day off, and repeat until the required count is reached. This handles consecutive holidays and any newly crossed weekend without a fragile add-one-calendar-day shortcut.

Without holidays, subtracting five prior weekdays from a weekday lands seven calendar days earlier. That is a different operation from counting five working dates inclusively ending on the deadline. Label your count so those conventions do not get mixed.

sections.heading: Worked example: fifteen working dates in four stages
body: Count November 20 as working date 15. Final QA uses November 19–20 (two dates). Stakeholder review uses November 12, 13, 16, 17 and 18 (five dates). Production uses November 3, 4, 5, 6, 9 and 10 (six dates). Scope uses October 30 and November 2 (two dates).

That is 2 + 5 + 6 + 2 = 15 working dates. October 30 through November 20 inclusive spans 22 calendar dates: 15 working dates, six weekend dates and the chosen November 11 day off. The elapsed midnight-to-midnight difference is 21 days; inclusive dates and elapsed duration are not the same count.

sections.heading: Put the plan into a calendar, then check capacity
body: Create the agreed deadline and the stage boundaries. Reserve actual work intervals on the eligible dates; counting a day as available is not proof that eight hours are free. Check meetings, partial days and who is responsible for each handoff.

Google and Outlook document recurring-event controls, including choosing where a series ends. An RFC weekday pattern selects weekdays but does not import your holiday policy. Review every occurrence around the days off.

If you delete one recurring occurrence, that removes a date rather than automatically shifting all later work. The source service may represent an exception differently internally; do not claim every GUI deletion literally writes an EXDATE file.

cells: Oct 31; Nov 1, 7, 8, 14, 15 weekends; Nov 11 chosen day off

practical: Define workdays, days off and the cut-off hour.
State inclusive counting or prior-day subtraction.
Walk dates backward and skip every ineligible date.
Check real capacity before saving execution blocks.

faq.q: Can I add one calendar day per holiday to a weekday formula?
faq.a: That shortcut can cross another weekend or another excluded day. Walk the eligible dates again instead.

faq.q: Does a Monday–Friday recurrence exclude public holidays?
faq.a: No. You need an explicitly confirmed holiday list and exceptions or separately bounded work blocks.

calendar-travel-time-versus-separate-buf.title: Calendar travel time or separate buffers? Check both journeys
calendar-travel-time-versus-separate-buf.short: Travel Time vs Buffer Event Blocks
calendar-travel-time-versus-separate-buf.description: Separate a travel reminder, booking-page buffer and Busy calendar block. Plan an outbound and return journey without promising universal availability blocking.
calendar-travel-time-versus-separate-buf.lede: A 14:00–15:00 visit with thirty minutes of travel each way occupies 13:30–15:30 in your personal plan. The shared meeting, a travel reminder and the availability used by a booking page are separate things. Check each rather than assuming one field covers both journeys.

sections.heading: What the documented controls actually say
body: Apple’s Mac event guide documents a Travel Time menu and warns that its value does not update automatically after a location change. That alone does not establish how a Google or Exchange availability service interprets the field, or prove a return trip has been reserved. Inspect the saved event and return window explicitly.

Google’s appointment-schedule guide describes Buffer time as adding time between appointments. This is a booking-schedule control, not evidence that the same time becomes a separate Busy event for every internal scheduling tool.

sections.heading: A worked three-block plan
body: For the illustrative 14:00–15:00 visit, place personal outbound travel at 13:30–14:00 and return travel at 15:00–15:30. Meeting 60 minutes + outbound 30 + return 30 = 120 minutes total. These durations are assumptions for the plan, not navigation estimates.

Keep the invitation at the actual agreed 14:00–15:00 time. Separate personal buffers avoid telling guests that the meeting itself starts at 13:30. If time or venue changes, review both travel blocks and any native Travel Time value.

sections.heading: Busy indicates availability; it is not an enforcement guarantee
body: RFC 5545 describes VEVENT and its TRANSP setting: opaque events can be considered in busy-time searches; transparent events do not block them. The standard does not guarantee that every provider reads every calendar, imports every field, or rejects conflicting invitations.

Save buffers in a calendar that your intended scheduling or booking flow actually checks. For Google appointment schedules, the availability-checking calendar choices also matter. Test a neutral block from the booking page or with a consenting colleague rather than declaring all clients protected.

sections.heading: Check details and visibility separately
body: Use a neutral travel-block title if route details are unnecessary. Inspect both item visibility and calendar sharing; an ICS CLASS value alone is not a universal access-control guarantee.
Keep this availability check separate from route/weather planning. The existing journey-planning guide addresses estimates and conditions; this guide focuses on which record a booking flow sees.

cells: Saved Busy state and calendar included by availability tool
Return window visible to the intended availability check
Spacing on that booking page; do not infer a separate global Busy event

practical: Keep the shared meeting at the agreed time.
Plan outbound and return intervals explicitly.
Check saved calendar, availability and sharing.
Test the actual booking flow after an edit.

faq.q: Does a travel-time menu prove the return trip is blocked everywhere?
faq.a: No. Inspect the return period and the exact calendar/availability service. Add and verify a separate personal block when needed.

faq.q: Does Busy stop someone sending me a conflicting invitation?
faq.a: It can inform availability checks; it is not a universal invitation-rejection rule.

alternating-a-b-week-school-timetable-ca.title: Alternating A/B week timetable: decide what a holiday skips
alternating-a-b-week-school-timetable-ca.short: Week A / Week B Timetable & Holidays
alternating-a-b-week-school-timetable-ca.description: Plan an every-two-weeks timetable around a one-week break. Compare a fixed calendar cadence with a paused teaching cycle and verify the first weeks after it.
alternating-a-b-week-school-timetable-ca.lede: A two-week recurrence keeps counting calendar weeks even when a class is removed. If a school pauses its A/B rotation during a holiday, deleting the holiday’s lessons alone will not create the intended post-break timetable. Confirm the school’s published schedule first.

sections.heading: Two recurrence patterns, one policy question
body: RFC 5545 can express weekly recurrence with INTERVAL=2. Outlook’s guide explicitly gives an every-other-Monday example. Google documents choosing the repeat frequency and ending date. The particular school decides whether a holiday consumes a rotation week; the calendar standard does not.

For this fictional Monday-only class example, A starts November 2, 2026 and B starts November 9. Both repeat every two weeks. November 23–27 is a chosen one-week break, and the example’s second teaching block ends December 18. This is not a real school holiday calendar.

sections.heading: Fixed calendar cadence: remove the break, keep the phase
body: With no re-anchoring, A would occur November 2, 16 and 30, then December 14; B would occur November 9 and 23, then December 7. Removing B on November 23 leaves November 30 as A.

RFC EXDATE removes matching recurrence instances; it does not restart the two-week interval. A provider’s single-occurrence deletion can implement an exception without literally exposing an ICS file, so verify the resulting dates in the source account.

sections.heading: Paused teaching cycle: bound and restart deliberately
body: If the school instead requires November 30 to be B, bound the pre-break series to the final teaching date before the break, then create post-break B on November 30 and A on December 7, each repeating every two weeks through December 18. Inspect for duplicates from any old unbounded series.

Use the editor’s supported ending-date control. If generating raw ICS, UNTIL has value-type and UTC requirements depending on DTSTART; do not write a placeholder such as UNTIL=Nov 20. The COUNT/UNTIL guide explains those requirements.
For classes on several weekdays, create the actual weekday/time records, not a single Monday class and an assumption that the rest appear. Use the published timetable to verify each one.

sections.heading: Verify the first two teaching weeks after every break
body: In the fictional example, fixed cadence produces A on November 30 and B on December 7. A paused cycle produces B on November 30 and A on December 7. That pair of dates is a more reliable check than a vague label such as odd week.

An even two-week break preserves the phase difference under these two explicitly defined models; an odd one-week break changes it. Partial-week closures, day rotations and school-specific resets need their own published rules.

practical: Read the school’s actual first post-break timetable.
Choose the intended cadence before creating series.
Bound old series before re-anchoring to avoid duplicates.
Verify the first two post-break teaching weeks.

faq.q: Why does deleting the break not swap A and B?
faq.a: An excluded occurrence does not reset the recurrence interval. Restart at the intended post-break anchor if that is what the school publishes.

faq.q: Can every school use the same two-week rule?
faq.a: No. A day rotation, partial-week closure or school-specific reset can follow a different policy. Use its official timetable.

sources.label: RFC 5545: weekly interval and UNTIL types
